items.author: @levie
items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: Coding gives you a window into what the future will look like for a large amount of knowledge work. The first step for most jobs is that we go from doing most of the research, typing, and value creation manually (even if it’s using digital tools) to soon coordinating the work that agents are doing. Next, as this step itself becomes redundant or slows down what agents are capable of, we will be giving agents goals to optimize against and they’ll go off on and increasingly solve larger problems for us. This may at first blush look like something whose impact gets stuck with coding, but actually a large percentage of knowledge work may eventually just converge with this form factor due to the massive productivity gains that can be generated. Agents will use computers, leverage our existing tools or write new ones, and write code on the fly to solve larger swaths of knowledge work. So even if a task today doesn’t seem to be “coding” directly, the task may eventually fold into being coding adjacent. Manufacturing, architecture, life sciences, material sciences, cyber, and on and on. One big hurdle in the way ultimately will be that much of this work remains non-verifiable, so humans will be even more in the loop than they are in coding. But the part that they can hand off will just get bigger and bigger over time as the models are more capable. So in short, pay attention to coding and you’ll get a sense for where work is going.

items.text: AI native teams will eventually force the surrounding organization to become AI native too. Take software development. coding velocity is way up thanks to AI, while actual shipped products and business impact are unchanged in most companies. That’s cos the surrounding system of experimentation tooling, evaluation, launch processes, and gtm are outdated. It’s like sticking a Ferrari engine in a sedan and racing it on Indian roads. The engine can rev faster but the car speed is limited by its system and environment. AI native companies were built ground up for this new way of building and shipping. They’re also able to shed suboptimal processes faster. Market forces will quickly force all companies to adapt or perish. If you’re solving this for your company: map out your product lifecycle and rebuild it ground up - tooling, team structure, gtm, everything.

items.title: How Clay Builds GTM Agents — Jeff Barg, Head of AI
items.excerpt: Open video on YouTube ↗ Clay wants you to get about the same results whether you use its own agent or point Claude Code at Clay. Usage is already split close to 50/50 between Clay’s agent and outside harnesses. In this episode, we chat with Jeff Barg, Head of AI at Clay, about what it takes to build go-to-market infrastructure that any agent can use. Jeff joined Clay when it acquired Avenue , the ops alerting startup he cofounded. At the time, Clay had about 50 people, and Avenue had five. AI was already a big part of how Clay thought about its product, but nobody there worked on AI. Since then, the business has grown roughly 10x, and the team is up to around 600 people. In September, Clay raised $115 million at a $7.1 billion valuation . By Jeff’s napkin math, it would cost about $1,500 to check all 40 million companies in Clay’s database against your ideal customer profile with a classifier like TypeSafe’s Jev. Models have been acing Clay’s lead-qualification evals for about a year now. Jeff sees more value in using frontier models for orchestration and deep research. We also talk about why customers hate picking a model, how Clay plans to pick one for them, and why the team still runs its agents on a system it built with BullMQ, without Temporal or LangGraph. Jeff tells us what happened when OpenAI called off Clay’s ChatGPT apps launch with two days to go. We get into why customers hated Workflows at first, how agents came to build most workflows, and when post-training pays off. We also talk about why agents still can’t debug other agents, even as Clay’s agent can coun…

items.title: Stop Building Software Factories — Justin McCarthy, Diffusion
items.excerpt: Most of the time you don't know what you want yet, so putting new ideas through a factory wastes time and tokens. Justin McCarthy, founder and CEO of Diffusion, argues for brownfield factories instead: continuous loops that keep the promises of software customers already pay for, getting faster, cheaper and safer around the clock. He explains why these factories simplify with every model release and why one takes about a week to stand up. Then he raises the stakes: with code now abundant, engineers need to build a demand factory that finds what customers will actually buy. items.title: How 21 People Built a $100M+ Agent Company — Quinn Slack, Amp
items.excerpt: Amp spun out of Sourcegraph with 21 people and, unable to hire for a year, was forced to work in a radically different way. Quinn Slack explains what that looks like: no task tracker, no PMs, one meeting a week, everything done in the agent, and tiny monitored pushes instead of big releases. He shows Amp's bug-report loop that fixes the issue and emails everyone affected, why they built their own CRM instead of using Salesforce, and how a company with more than $100M in ARR runs 40 to 50 times more efficiently. His advice: get out of the cage. items.title: 1,000 Claude Agents Formalized Fermat's Last Theorem — Lance Martin, Anthropic
items.excerpt: A team of 1,000 Claude agents formalized Fermat's Last Theorem in Lean over about 30 hours, using nothing but Git and a database, with no domain-specific harness and no human steering on the solution. Lance Martin shows how the lead agent built its own coordination tables and how the team reassigned itself as the work progressed. Then he turns to memory: why stronger models know what to write down, how Claude's Pokemon memory got tighter from Sonnet 3.7 to Fable 5, and how "dreaming" over transcripts fixes poisoned memories and builds better wikis. items.title: The Revolution vs The Renaissance — Thariq Shihipar, OpenAI
items.excerpt: AI can make software cheap enough to produce by the thousand and still give you more time to make one thing feel right. At AI Engineer CODE, Thariq Shihipar shows how those two futures can coexist. In his fighting game, he edits the size of a rock in the /human folder and immediately tries the throw. He also built a Mac Dock that switched modes, used it, and realized he cared more about noticing when he got distracted. We get into what Thariq changed his mind about with coding agents, how a decision model can choose from actions a designer defines, and who gets to decide which experiments deserve the compute. Thariq announced his move to OpenAI after we recorded. Sponsored by Jira by Atlassian. Learn more at jira.dev . items.text: This wouldn’t have sounded possible a year ago, but it’s becoming much more reasonable now that you can get 10X output gains based on the latest in AI model and harness progress. The result is that teams within the same company are driving very different levels of output based on how they’ve adopted AI. This is a different phenomenon from other tech. Typically in the economy you think of technology adoption rates on a per firm basis, because the company generally adopts a relatively standardized approach to doing the new tech thing. Like “that company has gone digital or adopted the cloud”. So generally the uplift across teams is more or less the same across teams. AI is starting to look quite different. Even within the same company you can have a 10X delta between the lowest and highest adopters of AI and the impact they’re seeing. The teams that are able to actually figure out how to redesign their processes to best deploy agents in their workflows can see up to an order of magnitude jump in productivity depending on the job function. Right now this is heavily concentrated in coding, but more work will become coding adjacent so we can expect similar results elsewhere too. This is going to definitely lead to some wild dynamics within companies.

items.author: Simon Willison
items.subtitle: Simon Willison
items.title: Three LLM inflection points in twelve months
items.excerpt: I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months. Here's the video of the talk. In this post I'm going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply. Coding agents in November 2025 Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5 . With hindsight, this was a consequential model. In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said: Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach. This held up. Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025. Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn't been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn't feel reliable enough - I had to correct it often enough that it didn't feel like a clear accelerant. The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right . It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself. Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect…
items.summary: 回顾过去一年，Claude Opus 4.5的发布是AI编码领域的关键转折点，标志着Agent已能处理复杂的多系统Bug并进行自主权衡。

He explains why the team made JavaScript faster instead of rewriting Claude Code in Rust, why tests that predate the project are what make agent-written code trustworthy, and what he actually does all day while 140 agents write code. items.title: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer
items.excerpt: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer GLM 5.4 is now available from Chinese AI lab Z.ai. It's their first model to use a looped transformer architecture, which they describe like this: In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count. This is the second mention of looped transformers I've seen in the past week - the first was Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines Lab on November 20th, who said: Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. GLM 5.4 is not yet available as open weights: We plan to open-source the model weights responsibly after completing necessary safety hardening. I tried it out using the Z.ai API, for which I had to sign up for their Coding Plan subscription because 5.4 cannot currently be accessed through the regular API. It turns out both coding plan and regular API share the same OpenAI-compatible Responses API (at https://api.z.ai/api/v1 ), and the API key for the coding plan worked with that and gave me access to the new model. I built a llm-glm plugin , then realized that llm-zai by Tommy Hughes already exists! I've shipped mine purely because llm-zai doesn't yet support the…

items.title: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery
items.excerpt: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries: With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library . It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians. Here's the digitized sketchbook . Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work. Are historians due for a round of Deep Blue ? Mark thinks it will be mild: But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we’ll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. To be fair, that crisis will almost certainly be less profound for us than it is for math. The problem in mathematics, of course, is that solving hard math problems was the whole game. Historians…

items.title: Ladybird's first alpha release
items.excerpt: Ladybird is an astonishingly ambitious project: a new browser, in 2026, with its own implementation of most of the key components - HTML parsing, CSS engine, layout, JavaScript, even WebAssembly. It still uses a few external components - things like HarfBuzz for text shaping, Skia for 2D graphics, ffmpeg for video, and SQLite for the things you do with SQLite. items.excerpt: Release: datasette-charts 0.1a0 I've been thinking about this problem for over a year now, but on Sunday I finally fired up Claude Fable 5.2 to build an initial prototype. The prototype went so well that this is now a full plugin. You can try it out in Datasette Lite here . It looks like this: The new charts plugin works against any table or arbitrary SQL query in Datasette. It defines several different chart types (using vendored D3 , Observable Plot , and topojson-client ), each with a set of heuristics for identifying when they might be a good match for a specific set of rows. Those suggestion thumbnails at the top are actual visualizations driven by the data, and selecting one pulls up the full chart along with tools for modifying it. You can also manually construct a chart from scratch. As with other Datasette visualization plugins, the current state of your chart is persisted in a #fragment in the URL - so you can bookmark charts or share them with others. The most important feature is that the charts take all rows into account . Previous charting plugins like datasette-vega would only show charts for the current page of results, generally up to 100 rows. The new plugin compiles each chart to a SQL query that aggregates across the entire result set (potentially millions of rows) using GROUP BY, time bucketing, and window functions. Each query returns a result capped at 5,000 rows, suitable for display on the chart. The plugin uses sampling to help suggest charts for larger tables without evaluating the full result set. items.excerpt: Release: datasette-charts 0.2a0 I introduced this new charting plugin for Datasette yesterday . Today it's gained integration with Datasette Agent , so now you can ask chat for a chart and it will create one for you using the same underlying chart suggestion and generation tools. Here's a demo video, recorded on agent.datasette.io where you can sign in with GitHub to try the plugin yourself: Download the video (MP4) I prompt Datasette Agent to "Use #stats to show sqlite-utils downloads over time as a chart" - where typing "#stats" opens a table search box. It shows me a chart inline in the chat, and when I click "Open in the chart builder" it opens the chart in a panel along with the table page. I use the table page to switch to a chart of "datasette", then when I ask the agent "what does the chart show?" it notices that I changed the content in the panel and describes the new Datasette chart to me. Here's a Markdown export of the chat from the video. Tags: datasette-agent , datasette , visualization , datasette-charts , sqlite

items.excerpt: Congrats to Sierra on tripling last year’s $10B valuation , and to Z.ai for releasing GLM 5.4 , their first looped transformer following Thinking Machine’s much smaller Inkling Mini 2 from last week. However all these are outshone by today’s twin title stories… Jensen Huang is back . Eleven days after announcing his resignation , Nvidia announced his return as CEO, president and member of the Board of Directors. View post on X ↗ The board voted unanimously after more meetings with Jensen on Sunday and said it received input from senior U.S. officials (aka the Treasury Secretary and the President dialing into the board meeting ). Colette Kress remains CFO, the independent directors’ investigation continues, and Jensen’s Senate hearing is still due in 8 days. Nvidia also formed a board committee for national security and export control. As Matt Levine points out , with the firing AND the rehiring by this board with involvement from the government, the investigators are now being put in a position of having had the outcome somewhat predetermined for them, because both have demonstrated that they did not need to wait for any further evidence to come to light. items.title: Build the Workshop Before the Software Factory — Armin Ronacher, Earendil
items.excerpt: Earendil's Pi coding agent has the same core tools it had a year ago, yet it does far more because the models got better. Armin Ronacher shows his own session data: fewer corrections, tasks running 14 minutes instead of two and a half, and 141 projects started but only 10 to 15 kept alive. His case: human attention is still the limit, so build a workshop that produces excellent software before building a factory that produces more of it. He also covers knowing when to push back on an agent, open formats, durable agents and code mode. items.title: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer
items.excerpt: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer GLM 5.4 is now available from Chinese AI lab Z.ai. It's their first model to use a looped transformer architecture, which they describe like this: In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count. This is the second mention of looped transformers I've seen in the past week - the first was Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines Lab on November 20th, who said: Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. GLM 5.4 is not yet available as open weights: We plan to open-source the model weights responsibly after completing necessary safety hardening. I tried it out using the Z.ai API, for which I had to sign up for their Coding Plan subscription because 5.4 cannot currently be accessed through the regular API. It turns out both coding plan and regular API share the same OpenAI-compatible Responses API (at https://api.z.ai/api/v1 ), and the API key for the coding plan worked with that and gave me access to the new model. I built a llm-glm plugin , then realized that llm-zai by Tommy Hughes already exists! I've shipped mine purely because llm-zai doesn't yet support the…

items.title: 12 Rules for a Software Factory That Doesn't Ship Slop — Dex Horthy, Factory
items.excerpt: The best model scores about 16% on Slop Code Bench, a new benchmark for how well agents evolve a code base over time. Dex Horthy uses that data to argue that software factories aren't new: they are good engineering with agents doing the building. He lays out 12 practices, from forward and back pressure to planning, visual alignment, lint rules against slop and a unified forge. Then he launches the Anti-Slop Manifesto and makes the case that reviewing work still matters. Read the manifesto: https://slopmanifesto.com Speaker info: - https://x.com/dexhorthy - https://factory.ai Timestamps: 0:00 - 12 factor factories and the war on slop 0:57 - Slop Code Bench: the best model scores 16% 1:42 - Software factories are just good engineering 4:01 - Forward pressure and back pressure 5:31 - 12 practices for software factories 6:16 - Know your enemy: models don't maintain code 9:20 - Plan before you build 10:50 - Align visually and let agents test 11:35 - Fight slop with lint rules 12:20 - Feature flags, evals and a unified forge 13:05 - What you can't buy 14:39 - The Anti-Slop Manifesto 18:24 - Why reviewing still matters

items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: Yes to all of this. As agents take on more and more long running project work, and you have swarms of agents that parallelize work against a goal, the agent harness and architecture for orchestration will have to evolve. One of the biggest shifts is how those agents collectively share their knowledge, keep track of the tasks, and also coordinate with human users. This in theory is technically straightforward, but there’s a ton of complexity to get right to ensure agents can both get access to the revenant resources without too much or little exposure. There are a lot of lessons to pull from based on how people already do this kind of work together (people share their files, have computers to work with, community in chats and inboxes, and so on). But equally the primitives need to be able to enable this work at a throughput far higher than people, and in a world where agents can much more easily become a vector of security risk. Going to be super fun building out this next generation of how agents operate. Lots of opportunity here both for horizontal and vertical specific approaches to bring this to life.

items.text: "I believe frontier model developers should jointly endeavour to establish shared norms for how to evaluate such models and red-team safety cases for them by the time they are first used, including shared transparency standards. I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone (such as the development of a successor to CoT monitors). That is, I’d like an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, measured by some key metric we can track across labs, and what concretely we’d need to achieve before going beyond it."

items.title: Build the Workshop Before the Software Factory — Armin Ronacher, Earendil
items.excerpt: Earendil's Pi coding agent has the same core tools it had a year ago, yet it does far more because the models got better. Armin Ronacher shows his own session data: fewer corrections, tasks running 14 minutes instead of two and a half, and 141 projects started but only 10 to 15 kept alive. His case: human attention is still the limit, so build a workshop that produces excellent software before building a factory that produces more of it. He also covers knowing when to push back on an agent, open formats, durable agents and code mode. Speaker info: - https://x.com/mitsuhiko Timestamps: 0:00 - Build the workshop before the factory 1:43 - The harness didn't change, the models did 3:17 - Agents now run 14 minutes per task 4:47 - Human attention is the limit 6:17 - 141 projects started, 15 maintained 7:47 - Knowing when to push back on the agent 10:02 - Executive summaries instead of reading code 11:32 - Uncontrolled growth and shared file formats 13:02 - Building software that strives for excellence 15:17 - Durable agents that suspend and resume 16:51 - Code mode and classifier models 19:06 - Build more ambitious software

items.text: This post nails why we why we should take the Riemann Hypothesis breakthrough very seriously, even beyond math. We’re entering an era where solving problems will look very different from how we solved them in the past. “This is not theory-building in the usual sense. It is something much weirder and more alien. The best human mathematicians know how to build theory, painstakingly, to reach a goal. But no human brain, on its own, is capable of creating a wormhole that requires a 25,000 page long tour through existing infrastructure with no obvious or realistic connection to the goal. But huge credit to Levent here: I think no current AI, on its own, is capable of this either.” It used to be the case that to solve a particular problem - code, life sciences, math, cyber, engineering, and so on - you were ultimately bound by how much information an individual or team could retain and understand about the space. More information or more team members don’t always help, because it gets harder to connect the dots or coordinate amongst everyone. AI changes that completely. For the first time ever we can decouple the human context limits and ability to work through information from our ability to drive productivity or discoveries. This is likely not just a small increase in the kinds of discoveries we can drive, but a qualitative shift in human output. Now every single form of prior art, insight, past research, past decision, or unrelated breakthrough, can be used for the discovery or creation of something new. This is useful for anything from cybersecurity to life sciences research. Agents will be able to correlate entirely unrelated work to a separate project; scan every bit of data in your enterprise for solving a problem; and so on. The solutions may not be as elegant as they were in the past, but we sure will have far more of them. We’re only in the first couple of months of actually understanding the implications of this but it’s clearly going to drive a lot of change.

items.excerpt: Within a few hours of each other ( timeline ), two mathematicians claimed independent proofs of the Riemann Hypothesis, the most famous open problem in mathematics ( Scientific American ). Levent Alpöge of Anthropic first made his Claude-driven proof in a note released with Lean code (1.3GB worth, ~250,000 page equivalent) rather than a full paper. Elliot Glazer confirms that the formalized statement is GRH and puts the chance of a Lean bug well under 1%. So if it finishes compiling with no extra axioms, it is probably correct, and no human will ever have read all of it… …prompting Alessandro Masullo to release his 940 page, 100% human , work in progress proof he had been working on for the last 12 years (and had been undergoing secret manual review and revision per Kevin Hartnett ). This is the third in the trilogy of frontier math breakthroughs, following from the Navier Stokes solutions and the Quasi-Riemann bounding, but it doesn’t feel over. OpenAI's September Navier-Stokes claim is still the cautionary tale: critics argued that its Lean proof did not match the natural-language result. Both AI-claimed Millennium Prize results will take years to verify. Apart from the incredible accomplishment of the most famous problem in mathematics, one cannot miss the contrast that the AI-written solution is probably correct but incomprehensible , and the other solution is probably technically incorrect but understandable . Sponsored by Agentfield.AI Open models are ready. Most coding harnesses aren’t. On DeepSWE, CodeAF finished #1 of ten on the same open model, ahead of Claude Co…

items.text: This year we’ve had a clear jump in model capability where instead of telling agents precisely what to do, it’s better to use these systems to solve problems you can’t easily define yourself. A year ago you’d need to very clearly tell agents the how to design and develop your product idea, or there was almost no chance of success. Now, increasingly, the agent likely can come up with a better implementation than you’d have thought of because you can have it connect the dots between a far greater solution space than you can. This will be increasingly true in basically every domain of kneeler work. We’re going to see this impact in finance, legal, life sciences, cyber, and many other spaces where no person can hold onto all the available relevant industry knowledge to think of the best solution. Ultimately this is going to reshape our relationship with AI and how we deploy agents in our work. It won’t be about explicitly telling them, but instead giving them goals and enough freedom to pursue them in the best way they can.

items.excerpt: Most developers still run coding agents locally and prompt them one at a time, which caps throughput and makes cost, security and governance hard to manage. Zach Lloyd, founder and CEO of Warp and former Google Docs engineering lead, defines a software factory as a code-defined, closed-loop system for continuously measuring and improving cloud coding agents. He walks through the stack: factories as code, recorded agent runs, sandboxed compute, swappable models and harnesses, and orchestration. He demos live team views, online evals, self-improvement through PRs and benchmarks on your own data. items.title: The War Against Slop and an Emerging Weapon to Fight it: Formal Verification
items.excerpt: The word of the year in the AI industry over 2026 has been “slop” — meaning low-quality output from a large language model. And with so much code being AI-generated now, avoiding slop has become a daily concern for software engineers. So how to do that? One way is to use formal verification systems , which use mathematical proofs and logic to verify the correctness of software or hardware. With AI’s growing prowess at solving math problems , there’s now a number of AI companies offering formal verification systems. They include Harmonic , Theorem , Axiom Math , and a new entrant called &Truth (pronounced ‘and truth’). In this article we’ll look at some of the approaches these companies are taking. How formal verification is used in software and AI today In order to better understand the landscape of formal verification systems, we spoke to one of its leading proponents: Clark Barrett , &Truth’s co-founder and co-CEO. He’s also Corbel Professor (Research) of Computer Science at Stanford and was the co-creator of cvc5 , a popular automated reasoning engine used in formal verification. Without getting too in the weeds, cvc5 is what’s called a “solver” for satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) , which Barrett says is widely used in companies like Amazon. For instance, cvc5 is used for specification analysis and test generation in Kiro , Amazon’s agentic development environment. “It's been fun to see my tools go from a good idea in the lab to cvc5 is now called billions of times a day in production pipelines at Amazon,” Barrett told us. items.title: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube)
items.excerpt: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube) Claire Vo runs ChatPRD , an AI platform that helps product managers "turn an idea into a spec". The product has been live since the GPT-4 era, and Claire has been building it in public for much of that time. In this YouTube video (see also the accompanying Twitter post ) Claire describes the flood of token fraud she has seen from groups abusing the product's free trial, sometimes just to get free AI usage but often to resell tokens or run other commercial enterprises on top of the ChatPRD agent. I am funding a international Roblox and Fortnite map studio. They run a loop of free trials and promo codes and then tunnel to my agent and use it to build Roblox and Fortnite maps. Apparently one of the common prompts Claire saw running through her agent involved SVGs of pelicans riding bicycles! Presumably the token scammers are using that to help sniff the underlying models - different model families have a definite signature, and I've used it like this in the past to try and guess the identity of stealth preview models on platforms like OpenRouter. items.text: One of the most impressive things I've seen, and I think this is an important advancement to the state of the art. Message boards were the enabling technology of both the Navier-Stokes math breakthrough and even the OpenAI/HuggingFace cyber feat. We built a message board infrastructure primitive. You can think of it as "headless Slack" (or remember IRC?) for agents. This is an important building block for software factories, self-optimizing systems, and scientific research, where the human prompting is just the seed of the system, and millions of agents can operate in a decentralized fashion. 𝚟𝚎𝚛𝚌𝚎𝚕 𝚋𝚘𝚊𝚛𝚍 is designed to be model, harness and hosting platform agnostic. Just bring your agents, give them our CLI, and watch magic happen.

items.title: 40x More Merged PRs With 2.7x the Engineers — Walden Yan, CPO, Cognition
items.excerpt: Cognition's merged PRs grew 40x in a year while its engineering team grew 2.7x. Walden Yan explains what changed: self-driving PRs by default, small pods that own everything from bug reports to QA, and a workflow run almost entirely from Slack. He covers running every service locally so agents can test, VMs rebuilt every hour, and agents that optimize the factory itself. Then he shows the next step: giving agents jobs instead of tasks, from tuning inference on new GPUs to an Android app maintained by Devin over 44 days. items.text: devin bots are multi-agent teams done right: - always on, proactive (but tuned for ROI) - own outcomes not tasks (but can collab w others) - manages teams of subagents (and reviews itself) - available everywhere (call text slack whatever hello @interaction) - consistent reporting thru interactive artifacts aka devinapps not long chats (HTML is all you need™ @trq212) this is the preview that @walden_yan gave at AIE. i've been trialing them for a week and i've been able to hand over my AEO, QA, cross-platform app porting, personal admin automation, and video editing work (also simultaneously moving from local agent worktree hell to cloud because ofc this is all cloud based thank god) hyped concepts this replaces: - /goal - "ultracode" / "ultra mode" - "loop engineering" - "agent to agent" - "agent swarms" - AI employees (see below) my main aha moment is that you don't want "AI Employees", we do not have agi yet and you will just fail if you overpromise/overexpect. what you want is the "just" the next level of abstraction above single tasks, and the overwhelming consensus I've had talking to everyone at the frontier of agents (yes incl cog competitors) is agent managers that own outcomes. incidentally, as an employer of humans it's also how i distinguish between someone who "has agency" (owns a problem area, finds issues and researches/brings solutions not problems) and who doesn't (only does precisely what i asked, not proactive, doesn't come up with suggestions i didn't think about). guess which one i value more lol. if youre a startup, reminder that Devin for Startups offers 65k in credits. apply via clanker

items.text: Agent swarms are the next scaling frontier for AI. For years, we’ve scaled intelligence by training larger models and giving them more time to think. But there’s another dimension: running many agents in parallel, exploring different approaches, challenging each other, and working together on solutions that no single agent could easily discover. OpenAI has already demonstrated the potential of this approach with breakthroughs in mathematics. Until now, experimenting with agent swarms yourself required building complicated orchestration infrastructure. Starting today on Replit, spinning up a swarm of agents is just one prompt away. Excited to see what people discover when we make collective machine intelligence programmable by anyone.

items.title: External sandboxes for coding agents
items.excerpt: External sandboxes for coding agents I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine. I worked on this project with Prime Radiant , the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects . My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox. To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations: external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly. external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance. external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package! Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code. The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still runnin…

items.author: @levie
items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: The chart of token spend per employee still has no ceiling in sight. And the closer you are to AI right now the deeper the sense is that we’re actually still in the early part of the curve of token use and adoption. This summer and fall’s model releases have continued to push the state of the art forward at a rate that already felt hard to maintain. As a result, for most productive use-cases the models are only now starting to actually work, and the feeling is that things will only accelerate from here. Coding, in retrospect, was basically trash even 12 months ago. Now it’s finally starting to get good. And now that coding is actually working, you’re getting tool and computer use, which open up a wide variety of knowledge work domains that weren’t possible to throw agents at before. Once you have agents that can code, use computers, leverage any tool out there, and understand a variety of domains, you can begin to throw them at a wide variety of knowledge work tasks that were hard to bring automation to across finance, life sciences, cyber, and more. So that brings agents to a broad set of work that we’re not really using them in yet at scale. Then comes the new form factors of agents. Agent swarms and background agents are going to eat up vastly more tokens than anything we can imagine. You’ll have agents running in most enterprises workflows processing data, validating work, doing research, providing decision support, and so on. And we’ll have swarms that fan out in parallel in areas like cyber, life sciences, coding, and more. So basically tokens are only going up from here.

Stability fell apart, but Anj Midha helped the core group spin out to BFL, which immediately built an incredible new imagegen model in the Flux series. But why are they now going into video and world models? Andreas gives an example you can try with one hand. If somebody tosses you a ball, your hand starts moving before the ball reaches you. A video shows you how it got there. The sound of impact can tell you when it hit something, even if the camera missed the contact. items.text: Introducing 𝚡𝚎𝚎𝚝: https://t.co/YaLEMbmKwf. A hermetic, pixel-perfect X post renderer in safe Rust / wasm. Zero browser, network, filesystem, system fonts. Renders a post to PNG in ~1ms (and 0.4 ms for @jack's "setting up my twttr" 😁). X is the global town square, and the medium is the message. Being able to preview what things will look like before posting is great for both humans and agents. Rendering with xeet is is 100x-1000x faster than booting up a browser and taking a screenshot, yet it's just as accurate. It reproduces Blink & HarfBuzz text shaping, 1/64px line breaking, RTL bidi, 28 Chirp font subsets, CJK/Math/Emoji fallbacks, "Show more" rules, etc. It's the kind of thing that would be wildly impractical, if not impossible, for a human engineer to pull off. Except 𝚡𝚎𝚎𝚝 is structured as an "autorepo." An oracle boots up Chrome, and verifies tens of thousands of text layout rules. A CI canary then watches the evolution of the original, and files signed PRs for agents to act on. It was conceived from the ground up around 'verification engineering', and the result speaks for itself. Enjoy!

items.text: AI models are inevitably going to keep getting better and better at all coding, tool and computer use, math, and other coding-related tasks. As a result, agents that can use software to do their work, or generate code from scratch, will improve at a faster rate than all other domains of knowledge work. On one hand that could mean that only a small subset of work can get automated. But probably what happens is that more and more work just becomes coding-shaped to adapt to what agents are good at. You can see it in the most recent examples of model releases in the past couple of months, where agents can generate code that becomes animated videos, games, 3D models for products, and so on. We also know that tool use gives agents the ability to work with much of the same software that people already work with. This helps in cyber, life sciences, finance, and a number of other domains. Our mental model traditionally has been that the models have to be able to know everything about anything to generate value, but in reality they *really* have to know how to use or generate software effectively combined with deep domain expertise to make the right judgment calls inside of workflows. When you have that powerful combination, almost everything else gets unlocked. This is why the acceleration of agents in knowledge work is only going to increase from here.

items.excerpt: Release: datasette-llm 0.1a11 datasette-llm is the intermediate plugin for Datasette that supports configuring LLMs for use with other Datasette plugins. This release adds support for OpenAI-compatible endpoints, so you can configure Datasette to use an LLM hosted anywhere that talks the OpenAI pseudo-standard web protocol. This means that if you're running local models with LM Studio or Ollama or llama.cpp (which just hit v1.0.0 ) you can run Datasette via uvx like this: wget https://datasette.io/content.db uvx --with datasette-agent datasette \ --root --secret 1 \ -s plugins.datasette-llm.default_model ' { "model": "lmstudio-qwen", "model_name": "qwen/qwen3.8-27b", "api_base": "http://localhost:1234/v1" } ' content.db And you'll get a local server running a Datasette Agent instance powered by your local model! items.text: Ok this is a big deal. We’ve been testing Gemini 4 Hydrogen in early access with the Box AI Complex Work Eval, and it’s a serious jump for fast models. Hydrogen is 5 percentage points better in accuracy than Gemini 3.8 Flash. That alone would be a great boost in capability, but possibly more importantly it did the tasks in less than half the time with about 12% fewer tokens on a typical task. For this eval, we give the Box Agent Hydrogen as a model for a series of complex tasks that represent real world work with enterprise documents across finance, consulting, life sciences, and other industries. Hydrogen will be a great model for a lot of efficient but complex tasks across these fields. Gemini team is definitely cooking. Hydrogen will be rolling out in the Box AI Studio shortly so any customer can build a custom agent with it.

items.text: What happens to frameworks in the agents era? to component libraries? to @shadcn? The answer is: we need to drill deeper. Delete the part, optimize, accelerate, automate. UI SDK is like the x86 instruction set for agents to build new UI components spontaneously. Agents are the new design engineers, and they're ready to build *anything* you ask, tailored to your usecase. High-level, rigid, single-framework abstractions are like kryptonite for what is essentially an infinite, untiring creation machine. I think we've found someone that allows us to have the cake and eat it too. A decades-long dream. UI SDK is packaged behaviors that give us accessibility, performance, cohesion, saving us tokens, errors and effort, but with absolutely zero limitations and tradeoffs for what UIs we can generate. Enjoy!

items.excerpt: The theme of day two of the AI Engineer Code Summit in San Francisco was increasing ambition using AI . And there have been few projects as ambitious as ArtCraft in the AI era. So far the fledgling company has released 17 open source versions of popular software tools , starting with a Photoshop alternative built from scratch in Rust called PhotoCraft . You could feel the excitement in the room this morning when ArtCraft founder and CEO Brandon Thomas presented a kind of manifesto for AI-based open source at AIE Code. When he mentioned that ArtCraft had cloned Adobe’s Acrobat, with a product called PdfCraft, it got a round of applause from the audience. In wrapping up, his rallying cries of “let's take back the entire internet” and “let's rebuild everything” were greeted with whoops and cheers. Thomas began his presentation by reliving the internet’s early history. In his view, the web started out with the right intentions, but things got screwed up once Web 2.0 hit the mainstream. “We had a bunch of chat applications that were completely open,” he said, regarding the 1990s internet. “So, IRC is like Discord, but you can spin up your own servers that you actually own. You can use whatever programs to automate them and interrogate them without rules.” His point wasn’t necessarily that everything was open source, but that web users could freely build things. With Flash, for example — a commercial animation tool eventually acquired by Adobe — “kids were making all kinds of animations.” When Web 2.0 came along, with its superior broadband and smartphones, “it brought everybody…

items.author: Richard MacManus

items.title: The Jev Revolution: What Engineers Are Already Building with System One Models
items.excerpt: Today at the AI Engineer Code Summit , the main theme was system one models — non-generative models that return structured choices, scores, or probabilities. They’re also typically much faster and cheaper than reasoning LLMs (a.k.a. system two models). And who better to give an inspirational rallying cry for system one models than Diogo Almeida , co-founder and CEO of TypeSafe AI . Almeida was lead creator of Jev , the product that kicked off this trend less than two months ago. Jev was an instant revelation for AI engineers when it was released in September. In a podcast with Latent Space on launch (which quickly became our most popular episode of the year), Almeida explained the core problem with making LLMs the heart of software: reliability . In his keynote at AIE Code today, he took it a step further by claiming that Jev is “reliable intelligence” that should be used for “just automating everything.” Integrating system one models into code Of particular interest to AI engineers is Almeida’s point that system one models should become integrated with code. As he put it in his keynote, “code is the language of automation , therefore you need to integrate with code.” Latent Space founder swyx interprets this as a call to “liberally sprinkle ‘System One’ model calls everywhere INSIDE application code to make smarter software instead of increasingly convoluted forms of ‘concat strings together and hope for the best" AI engineering.’” The term “smart software” was used throughout Almeida’s presentation. It sounds like the kind of term used by companies like Microsoft or IBM…

items.author: @danshipper
items.subtitle: Dan Shipper · ceo @every | the only subscription you need…
items.text: I look at what I do with Fable 5.2 in the cracks of my week and think: this would've taken five people and $200,000. Then I look at what my team does with the same AI. Last week, between meetings, I analyzed our customer survey, made a game for our team, spotted an opportunity to sell @Every to teams, built a CRM, and started reaching out. Look at that and you might ask: Why would I need a team at all? The chart seems to agree. On OpenAI's GDPval benchmark, AI went from beating human experts 12.4% of the time in 2024 to around 83% in 2026. That's the aggregate view of the future of work: gather a lot of data and extrapolate a trend line. But the aggregate misses something. To see it, you have to get intimate: zoom in on one real situation, with all its messiness, and extrapolate from there. We gave everyone at Every access to the same customer survey and the same AI models. • I found an opportunity to sell to teams. • @poojary_yash saw that first-time subscribers were churning because we send too much email. • @dabrundage noticed that many of our readers feel lonely: they're excited about AI, but people around them think they're crazy. • @jackcheng turned the results into a Claymation game show. Could you ask Claude to produce what each of them found? Maybe. But generating possibilities is cheap. Knowing which ones matter is hard. @hammer_mt ran an experiment to predict what I'd say in Slack. When Claude got 400 attempts, it produced an answer like mine 93% of the time. But when it had to rank its own answers, mine landed in its top 10% only around 60% of the time. Each person on a team is responsible for a different part of the world. That responsibility narrows where they look, and their perspective helps them decide what matters enough to act on. A team explores more possibilities than a single default prompt, and it can take responsibility for what it finds. The obvious objection: models will get better at ranking. I think they will. But people aren't frozen while that happens. Comparing 2026 Yash with 2027 Claude misses that there will also be a 2027 Yash, with another year of experience, using 2027 Claude. As models improve and spread, they raise the floor for everyone. The default answer becomes the baseline. The value is in using your perspective and responsibility to push past it. That's why I think we need to change how we measure AI. Instead of only asking how well a model performs on problems everyone agrees are worth solving, ask: How good is it at doing my work, from my perspective? The aggregate can show us the capability curve. The intimate helps us see what we might build, and who we might become, as we ride it. I presented this at Thesis: 2027. The full talk is on the Every podcast:

items.text: I scraped 803 companies sub-processors to investigate what AI native companies are using for their infrastructure.. Some interesting findings from the last time I did this in March: > 44% of companies list two+ model providers (up from 33%). Small n, but Anthropic grew twice as fast as OpenAI. > 86 pairs where each company names the other as a subprocessor (@AnthropicAI + @Cloudflare, @vercel + @spacexai) > 33% of companies list an inference provider (up from 22%). @modal continues to crush. > Chinese models are primarily coming through video (think Bytedance) rather than text (at least on the subprocessor lists) > @typesafeai is the breakout hit, going from 0 to many companies in a short period. Caveat: subprocessor lists tend to be a lagging indicator, but a sure shot way of knowing if the company is using something. You can find all the updated data, design and insights at deploygraph dot com. Feedback welcome!

items.text: There are basically two kinds of companies to build right now. 1. Diffusion of AI This is the "vertical SaaS" of today. There are a bunch of different models for it (FDE company, rollup, horizontal product) but ultimately it all boils down to the same thing: get AI diffused very close to where the work is being done. Profound, Cognition, Harvey etc. A lot of great companies will get built here. 2. Frontier of AI This is where the really interesting action is. Use AI to accelerate scientific progress, then build products from that progress. It is a harder category to see. But we are seeing a lot more of it at @spc: - Externa is adding hundreds of new chemical building blocks to proteins, so you can engineer a drug to match the disease instead of settling for what nature gave you. - Epana Bio is using genomics and AI to design autoimmune therapies that go after the cellular origin of the disease. - VenomicsAI is doing AI-accelerated drug discovery from venoms. - Equivariant is doing multi-physics modeling for the semiconductor industry. (There are always picks-and-shovels for AI as well. Lots of amazing companies in that category.) Category 2 is not well understood or much talked about externally. It should be because I think that is where the vast majority of model driven returns will come from.

items.excerpt: Our usual bar for making a fundraise a title story these days is a decacorn ($10B) valuation. We missed Mercor’s $10B Series C last year when it had less than $500m in revenue, but knew we wouldn’t have to wait too long til the next round, since it crossed $1B in Feb and $2B in June , it has now hit $3B annualized, surviving hacks : View post on X ↗ The company reports 5 million experts, and their TAM: “In the United States alone, there are more than 800 distinct occupations, each containing workflows that models have yet to be evaluated against.” And also this notable stat we are tracking: We’re seeing the impact of AI investment in our business. We already spend 3x as much on inference as on employee salaries, and it pays for itself by making our team better at their jobs . If that ratio holds as AI spreads through the rest of the economy, it points to something closer to double-digit GDP growth over the next five years, nearly 3x the rate we’re used to. We have yet to do a Mercor pod (will work on it!) but to better understand a data vendor business, you can look at our recent deep dive with Handshake AI , one of their competitors: AI News for 11/09/2026-11/10/2026. items.title: Your Spec Has Bugs. Catch Them Before Your Agent Codes. - Rajath Mahendrappa Kotyal, AWS
items.excerpt: Spec-driven development only works if the spec is right, and specs are full of quiet bugs: rules that can't both hold, missing failure cases, sentences with two meanings. Your coding agent will faithfully build every one of them. Rajath Mahendrappa Kotyal shows how Kiro catches these before any design or code is generated by pairing LLMs with SMT solvers, turning the model's own disagreement into a signal that a requirement is ambiguous. You'll also see where solvers beat LLM-as-judge, and where they don't. Rajath Mahendrappa Kotyal, AWS: https://aws.amazon.com

items.title: Agents Made Code Free. Maintaining It Didn't Get Cheaper. - Dmitry Buykin, Maersk
items.excerpt: Coding agents made writing code almost free, but maintaining it didn't get any cheaper. Dmitry Buykin shares what happens months in, once agents write most of a large production codebase: tests that pass while production breaks, work nobody asked for, rules that contradict each other, and sprawl no one can review. He covers the patterns that actually help, from replaying real tasks and expert-owned evals to runtime guardrails and weekly pruning, and closes with an 18-question checklist for auditing your own AI-coded repo. Dmitry Buykin, Maersk: https://x.com/tzakus | https://linkedin.com/in/buykin/

items.author: AI Engineer
items.subtitle: YouTube
items.title: 225,000 Lines of Tests, Written and Merged by Agents - Kush Agrawal, Duolingo
items.excerpt: Duolingo's iOS app has nearly 2 million lines of code, and its unit test coverage lagged far behind. Kush Agrawal walks through the autonomous pipeline that fixed it: scheduled workflows pick untested code, coding agents open pull requests, and a lifecycle manager monitors CI, fixes failures, runs AI review and merges, with engineers as the final reviewers. Since March it has merged more than 700 PRs and 225,000 lines of tests, raising overall app coverage from 11% to 24%. He covers the architecture, the guardrails, the failure modes, and how they're reusing the same loop for other migrations. Kush Agrawal, Duolingo: https://www.duolingo.com

items.author: @levie
items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: Agent swarms have the potential to drive yet another leap in output from AI. The impact will be a clear separation between teams that adopt this pattern of work and those that don’t. The progression has roughly been: chat gave us quick turn AI responses that let us work a bit faster, but we were still rate limited by our interactions; then agents that can go off and complete entire tasks for us, accelerating hours or days of work into minutes; to now swarms of agents that are goal seeking and will find any route to the successful completion of a project, where there’s no inherent limit to the productivity gains. We can imagine a future where, for any task in which value can be created within a self-contained digital environment, swarms will be able to complete the work faster than any other approach. Essentially any area where value creation is currently bound by the amount of research you can do, the amount of decisions made with a set of software tools, the amount of data processed or consumed, and the amount of code (or code adjacent) that can be generated. This means swarms will play a big role in game development, coding, trading, life sciences research, IT automation, cyber, math breakthroughs, animation, and plenty of other areas of work that have these characteristics. There’s a lot of opportunity to build the harnesses, applied AI products, and infrastructure for how these agents operate. And most importantly there’s a ton of opportunity for those that can wire up work in this way. It’s going to be an entire new field of FDE work available.

items.excerpt: AI Engineer Code Summit kicked off today with a series of workshops, including from leading frontier labs OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind. I attended the OpenAI workshop, intriguingly titled “New Ways of Working with Codex” and hosted by two of its Developer Experience engineers, Dominik Kundel and Charlie Guo . The past year in coding agents has been one of constant product upgrades by all the frontier labs. But not all of these changes have gone smoothly. The shift to cloud , for example, is still confusing to many users of Codex, Claude and Antigravity. An illustration of the evolution of Codex, shown at the OpenAI workshop today. We’ve also seen new ways to work with agents. Personal agents like OpenAI’s dots and Anthropic’s Claude Duet can assist between sessions, while voice mode gives developers another way to steer coding tasks. OpenAI’s workshop addressed all three, and I also had some followup questions on these topics for Kundel, after the session. Guo began the workshop by listing a selection of things they’ve shipped in Codex since the AI Engineer World’s Fair in June 2026. “I had to cull this list in order to make it fit on the screen because there were too many things to put in here ,” he said. “I think the team has been shipping at an unbelievable rate.” The awkward transition to cloud Codex launched in May 2025 as “a cloud-based software engineering agent that can work on many tasks in parallel.” But Kundel admitted that “it took a while for models and harnesses to equalize into something where we can build a really engaging experience.” In other wor…

items.text: BREAKING: @Google just dropped Gemini 4 Carbon. It’s a much better coder than Argon—but I’m probably keeping Argon for writing. We’ve been testing it at @every across coding, writing, design, and knowledge work. It can work for hours on an ambitious project, but it doesn’t always know when to stop. Here’s your day-zero vibe check: • Coding: On one run of our Senior Engineer benchmark, Carbon scored 44%, versus Argon’s 21%. A big improvement, though still middle of the pack. In a separate test, @hammer_mt gave it a backlog to work through. It identified 6 tasks as ready, then did 15—including work someone else was already doing. He stopped it after almost 4.5 hours. • Big builds: @RandyCounsman gave it 3D scans of our podcast studio and an equipment list. In one attempt, it built a browser-based model accurate enough to check whether new gear would fit without getting into the shot. He estimates Carbon also wrote about 95% of a big update to Everycut, our internal video editor. • Code quality: @kieranklaassen values its tests and documentation on large projects, including its record of approaches it considered and rejected. Fable remains his first choice, but Carbon has earned a place alongside it. The catch: It can produce huge files where Fable keeps things more modular. • Audio and video: Randy found it caught audio editing issues other models missed. Kieran handed it a recorded meeting and asked for shorts. It came back with 6 titled clips. • Design: @jackcheng got a hyperrealistic ginkgo-leaf app icon with details other models struggle with. Objects and 3D scenes look better than Argon’s. Interfaces split the team: Jack and Randy kept getting boxes within boxes, while @TylerNishida liked its ideas for new interfaces. Kieran says giving it design guidance makes a big difference. • Writing: Our editorial benchmark put Carbon and Argon about even. If you like Argon, you’ll probably like Carbon. But Carbon costs more, and I haven’t seen enough improvement to justify switching. My Reach Test: 🟨 I’ll use it sometimes. Give it one big job with a clear finish line, and review what comes back. It’s also worth trying as a second opinion, especially on audio and video. Full vibe check coming soon: https://t.co/Ch2pNl9Po5

items.excerpt: Editor’s note: With this post, we are launching a new series focused on trying new models and products with unbiased reviews. Reach out with suggestions to tips@latent.space. Naive-N0.5-Flash is a new open-weights model built for AI coding tasks and tuned to generate as many tokens per second as possible . It was developed by a Chinese company called NaiveAI , with the aim of speeding up engineering and research workflows so that teams can experiment, iterate and solve complex problems faster. The model is an evolution of Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.5 , which NaiveAI has trained further for long-context reasoning and paired with its own NaiveRT inference engine. Naive-N0.5-Flash arrives with a bold pitch: a model built largely by AI and trained to do AI research itself, with recursive self-improvement as the long-term goal. To see what changed, it helps to know where it started. MiMo-V2.5 is a 310B-parameter sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with 15B active parameters, trained on 48T tokens. Its language backbone inherits the hybrid design of MiMo-V2-Flash, which mixes sliding-window attention (SWA) with global self-attention. NaiveAI's recipe starts from those weights. Through continued, multi-stage training, the team adapted the checkpoint to DeepSeek Sparse Attention layers. According to the NaiveAI technical blog , this took roughly 3.25T additional tokens on top of MiMo's original 48T. About 3T of those additional tokens were trained at a fixed 1M context length and with a constant learning rate. Benchmarking NaiveAI vs. DeepSeek and Z.ai We benchmarked the ultrafast mode of Naive…

items.title: Your Agent Hates Your CLI - Ayush Bhardwaj, Allos AI
items.excerpt: An agent can hide a failed test behind a successful shell pipeline. It can also trim away the error message and confidently report that everything worked. Ayush Bhardwaj examined roughly 20,000 tool calls from his own coding sessions and found a product roadmap in the commands agents wrote immediately afterward. Repeated uses of head, tail, grep and Python showed where tools returned too much information, exposed the wrong fields, or made the agent reconstruct the same query again. The examples come from his own traces and his chat history CLI, which lets agents retrieve context from earlier coding sessions. The fixes are small and concrete: return the messages around a search match, offer compact search results, inspect several sessions in one call, and put a useful failure summary at the end of the output. But implementing a flag does little if the skill file still teaches the old interface. In Ayush's case study, agents kept passing a flag that did nothing until the instructions changed. He also explains how to turn recorded calls into replay tests, reserve examples for evaluation, and check whether better output actually improves answers and reduces turns. Smaller responses alone do not establish a faster or cheaper workflow. The useful feedback is already in the transcript: what the agent tried, what it discarded, and what it had to ask again. items.text: BREAKING: @AnthropicAI just dropped Claude Fable 5.2. It’s a paradigm-shifting model if you have a project ambitious enough to give it. We’ve been testing it at @every, and I’ve seen this crazy explosion of creativity on the team. People are making their own creative software, games for their kids, and documentaries instead of slide decks. Here’s your day zero vibe check: • Coding: @kieranklaassen built Everycut, a video editor with the features we use from Premiere, Descript, and other tools—all in one app, with an agent built in. The first version was live in 3 days, and we immediately used it for our internal show-and-tell. This feels like a new era of professionals building their own professional tools, tailored to exactly how they work. • Games and design: @jackcheng gave it a photo of his toddler’s messy playroom. It turned the actual toys into a playable racing game, with fun details like a stray shoe as an obstacle and a sippy cup as a power-up. • Knowledge work: @hammer_mt turned his research into a documentary. The model came up with interview questions, he answered them on camera, and it cut the footage together. He called this the most productive 3 weeks of his career. • A different way of working: Give it a big job and leave it running overnight or over a weekend. But tell it what “done” means: Mike found it could finish the build, then spend another day or two testing. Set the goal, the budget, and how much checking you need before walking away. • The catch: It’s slow and burns through tokens. Our early-access usage was free, and these projects would have been expensive at API rates. It’s 20% cheaper than Fable 5.1, but for everyday writing, emails, or quick back-and-forth coding, I’d usually reach for something else. The clearest signal: When our early access ended, @TylerNishida stopped working on some projects until he could get this model back. He didn’t want to build them with anything else. The best measure of a new model is whether it makes you try things you wouldn’t have tried before. Fable 5.2 absolutely does that. Here’s our full day-zero Vibe Check:

It turned the actual toys into a playable racing game, with fun details like a stray shoe as an obstacle and a sippy cup as a power-up. • Knowledge work: @hammer_mt turned his research into a documentary. The model came up with interview questions, he answered them on camera, and it cut the footage together. He called this the most productive 3 weeks of his career. • A different way of working: Give it a big job and leave it running overnight or over a weekend. But tell it what “done” means: Mike found it could finish the build, then spend another day or two testing. Set the goal, the budget, and how much checking you need before walking away. • The catch: It’s slow and burns through tokens. Our early-access usage was free, and these projects would have been expensive at API rates. It’s 20% cheaper than Fable 5.1, but for everyday writing, emails, or quick back-and-forth coding, I’d usually reach for something else. The clearest signal: When our early access ended, @TylerNishida stopped working on some projects until he could get this model back. He didn’t want to build them with anything else. The best measure of a new model is whether it makes you try things you wouldn’t have tried before. Fable 5.2 absolutely does that. Here’s our full day-zero Vibe Check:

items.title: Every Correction You Give Your Agent Is Data - Brian Douglas, Paper Compute
items.excerpt: A Rust program can compile and still violate the decisions an experienced teammate would catch immediately. Brian Douglas finds that missing knowledge in moments when engineers push back on their coding agents. At Paper Compute, he captures agent sessions, labels corrections and uses those traces to recover the reasoning that otherwise disappears inside a local coding harness. His example starts with a gap in his own Rust expertise: accepting plausible generated code leads to objections later, when a teammate reviews the pull request. Those earlier objections become useful training material only if someone preserves and labels them. Brian demonstrates session capture with Tapes and Paper Console, then runs a Twin Review prototype against a pull request using examples of a teammate's feedback. He discusses labels for pushback, successful sessions and regressions, and shows how the same records can support skills, evaluations or model adaptation. The prototype is a demonstration, not a measured comparison against an independent evaluation set, and Brian corrects himself during the recording to clarify that Twin Review is not publicly released because its data is sensitive. His practical starting point is simpler than training a model: collect the traces you already generate, find the corrections that encode your team's conventions, and turn those into a skill you can test. The durable asset is the connection between a decision, the expert's objection and the resulting outcome. items.title: Merge Is the Bottleneck - Prasanna Sankar, Vorflux
items.excerpt: A customer call ended with a bug, and an agent found the unfinished task in the transcript and screen recording. In Prasanna Sankar's account, it asked for permission to investigate, involved the responsible engineer, produced a pull request and drafted the customer followup after the fix shipped. That example captures where Vorflux's engineering work led: once agents can complete longer tasks, coordinating and starting the right work becomes its own bottleneck. Prasanna traces the progression from cloud coding sessions to persistent bots with a goal, an owner and a shared channel. The foundation is six practical problems: reproducing a working development environment, investing more effort in planning, dividing tasks with dependencies, testing without returning to a laptop, reviewing from multiple angles, and keeping changes mergeable as the base branch moves. Browser tests, recordings and staging links give people something concrete to inspect. The second half shifts from those coding workflows to on call, CI and project management bots that respond to signals already present in the company. Prasanna also describes the failure mode of indiscriminate automation: noisy alerts, unwanted pull requests and growing token bills. His proposed controls are budgets, visible work, named ownership and increasing responsibility as results justify it. These are lessons and examples from building Vorflux, with a clear acknowledgment that the bots remain fallible and some responsibilities still belong with people. items.title: Quoting Prompting Claude Fable 5.2
items.excerpt: Claude Fable 5.2 pays close attention to who owns the code it works on. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model tended to add to the existing structure when the prompt said nothing about ownership or presented the code base as someone else’s, even when that duplicated existing code. When the prompt said the code base was the model’s own, it often consolidated duplicated code and sometimes made related fixes without being asked. If you want the model to improve the structure as it works, say that the code is its own: You are the owner and long-term maintainer of this codebase, and its design is up to you. The ownership sentence makes the model much more likely to consolidate duplicated code into one shared function. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model consolidated duplicated code in under 10 percent of runs without the sentence and in about 75 percent of runs with it. — Prompting Claude Fable 5.2 , Anthropic documentation Tags: prompt-engineering , anthropic , generative-ai , ai , llms , claude-mythos-fable

items.title: Give Your On-Call Its Own AI Teammate - Swaapnika Motapothula, Chinmay Gandhi & Vlad Tsvang, Meta
items.excerpt: Twelve alerts fire at 2 a.m., and a useful assistant can still leave the engineer coordinating every step. Meta's on call team uses that illustrative scenario to explain a different design: one AI teammate per rotation, with shared context, its own identity, persistent memory and explicit limits on what it can do. Swaapnika Motapothula, Chinmay Gandhi and Vlad Tsvang describe a system that connects alerts, tickets, incident history and code changes instead of leaving each automation with its own isolated view. The goal is to bring a human a decision with supporting evidence and a proposed action. Their autonomy ladder starts with investigation, advances to drafting fixes for approval, and permits selected lower criticality work only when mistakes are cheap to detect and the agent has earned trust on that action. Critical production decisions stay with people, and code changes still go through normal review and continuous integration. The team explains the automation loops for triage, recovery from stuck runs, and shift handoffs, plus how team specific skills and memory carry expertise between engineers. Corrections reopen work and become new evidence, while memory entries can be promoted or retired. The examples show the intended experience rather than a measured time savings result: the speakers explicitly reserve that claim for a rigorous study. Their next steps focus on accepted mitigations, better feedback and earning further autonomy. items.title: I Let Agents Refactor My Codebase for 3 Weeks. Then I Read the Code. — Keiji Kanazawa, Microsoft
items.excerpt: A coding agent wired unit tests to production inference, then ran them about 30 times. Keiji Kanazawa had spent three weeks letting coding agents refactor a personal research assistant. A bad digest sent him looking for a trace, and he discovered the "agent" was still a deterministic workflow. Skills had no SKILL.md, different architectural concepts were aliases for the same thing, and a daily reflection job was producing empty reports. He had approved plans without checking whether the implementation meant what its labels promised. He rebuilt around an explicit agent runtime, clearer specifications and goal rubrics, comparing four frameworks before selecting tools for his own needs as a product manager. The working example is a video deep dive agent that extracts 440 keyframes from an inference lecture, pairs blackboard equations with explanations and lets him question individual sections. The result generalizes to slide decks, coding demos and terminal recordings. He iterates on an evaluation rubric, lets agents optimize against it and uses adversarial reviews between coding agents. The rubrics need scrutiny too: one was tuned to a single lecture and failed on five other videos. His answer to the code reading debate is to own the goals and evaluation loop while continuing to delegate most implementation. items.title: Engineering Agency out of the Happy Path — Matthew Jewkes, Standard Cybernetics
items.excerpt: A biopharma automation reached 99.95% accuracy on its business critical tasks after the team separated actual errors from ambiguous cases and exceptions. Matthew Jewkes describes building that system at Clarivate, where indexing drug development documents meant handling tens of thousands of new tasks a month. An early agent approach reached around 80% to 83%. Working through 1,000 evaluation examples with domain experts exposed three different problems: the model could be wrong, the organization could lack an agreed answer, or genuinely new science could require judgment. Each needed its own route. The routine path became a tightly specified automation, with uncertain and unusual cases escalated instead of pushed through. The larger payoff was recovering expert attention. Once routine decisions were handled, the remaining cases could be grouped for deliberate review: critical exceptions to clear, ambiguous low value work to freeze, and unusual demand that might justify a new product. One expert used that structured backlog to form an investment thesis before a major customer raised the same need. Jewkes lays out where the investment makes sense, how much evaluation work high reliability requires and why organizational ownership and trust matter alongside engineering. His bet is that companies will gain more from managing collective attention and judgment than from choosing a particular orchestration framework. items.title: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind
items.excerpt: Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work - I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today's coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions. They're too good at describing the work The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That's a lot of information to absorb. It's not necessarily slop, but it reads like slop! It's very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as "I'm not reading all of that". It doesn't matter how accurate or useful the information is, I'm instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me! I want human editorial judgement. I want someone to have thought just long enough about the PR to give me a human-approved introduction that helps me understand, at a high level, what the PR is for and whether it deserves more of my attention. I think I've found a low-effort way to do this that feels right. Hide most of it in a details/summary The HTML <details><summary> elements render as a collapsed heading (the summary) that can be expanded to view the larger piece of text. The code looks like this: < details > < summary > Claude Opus 5.5…
